clue.text: It's not concrete we have to remove

explanation.surface: Someone explains that taking concrete away is what is required of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstract as an adjective means theoretical, without physical substance; as a verb it means to take away or extract.

clue.text: A third-rate divine right.?

parts.note: C is the third grade, after A and B
a divine is a clergyman, such as a curate

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a mediocre clergyman has a sacred entitlement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divine' here is a noun, a member of the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: Accurate means correct, exactly right.

clue.text: One 'century for one club perhaps

parts.note: single means one
a ton is a hundred, as a century of runs in cricket

explanation.surface: A cricketer makes a solo hundred for his team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' is the card suit: in bridge a singleton is the only card held in a suit, so one lone club is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A singleton is a lone card of its suit in a hand, as a single club would be.

clue.text: "April … stirring Dull —— with spring rain" (Eliot)

parts.note: the missing word completes a line from the opening of T. S. Eliot's poem The Waste Land

explanation.walkthrough: The Waste Land opens 'April is the cruellest month ... stirring / Dull roots with spring rain'.
explanation.definitionFit: The underground parts of plants, which spring rain wakes in the poem.

clue.text: Hasty and possibly sour in utterance

indicators.note: one piece is placed within the other, so the rearranged letters sit inside

parts.note: a cry is a vocal utterance

indicators.note: possibly signals another arrangement of the letters of sour

explanation.surface: A remark made in haste may come out sounding bitter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sour' sits in the surface as a taste of the voice; 'possibly' makes it anagram fodder, and 'in' sets the result inside the cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Cursory means quick and superficial, done hastily.

clue.text: John Peel's drink ?

parts.note: John Peel of the hunting song rode after foxes, so he was one who rode in pursuit; the same word names a small drink taken after spirits

explanation.walkthrough: John Peel is the huntsman of the English song 'D'ye ken John Peel', a man who chased foxes; the word for such a pursuer is also a drink downed after another.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunter in pursuit is one who chases, and a drink taken after a stronger one shares that name.

clue.text: Guns of a size worth ordering

indicators.note: putting letters in a new order rearranges the letters of size and worth

explanation.surface: Artillery pieces large enough to be worth buying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordering' looks like placing an order to buy, but it rearranges SIZE and WORTH.
explanation.definitionFit: Howitzers are short artillery guns firing shells at a high angle.

clue.text: This daddy needed to produce the lolly

definitions.text: This daddy needed to produce the lolly

parts.words: This daddy needed to produce the lolly
parts.note: a rich older man who lavishes money on a young lover is called by this word plus daddy; it is also what a sweet lolly is made of, and slang for money, which lolly also means

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lolly' is British slang for money as well as a sweet on a stick; the word wanted makes both, and prefixes 'daddy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar is the sweet substance a lolly is boiled from, and also old slang for cash.

clue.text: Defend 'oneself against a weird sister

indicators.note: weird suggests something strange or twisted, so the letters of sister are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone fights off an attack by an eerie sister, as from Macbeth's witches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weird sister' recalls the witches in Macbeth; 'weird' rearranges SISTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To resist is to withstand or fight off.

clue.text: Razes standards

explanation.surface: Someone demolishes the norms.
explanation.definitionFit: To level a building is to flatten it, and levels are standards or grades of attainment.

clue.text: Crowd gets lessons in dishonesty

parts.note: a con is a swindle, a piece of dishonesty
a course is a series of lessons

explanation.surface: A gathering of people is offered training in how to cheat.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'lessons in dishonesty' reads as one idea, a training course in conning; the charade follows that reading, and 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A concourse is a large gathering or throng of people.

clue.text: Death to the sinner, Paul told the Romans

definitions.text: Death to the sinner, Paul told the Romans

parts.words: Death to the sinner, Paul told the Romans
parts.note: in his Epistle to the Romans, Paul says sin pays its servants in death: that payment is the word wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Romans 6:23 reads 'the wages of sin is death', so what death is to the sinner is his pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Pay earned for work done, here the death that sin earns according to Paul.

clue.text: Theatrical, functions?

parts.note: 'functions' looks like events or parties put on by the theatre, but it means the parts actors play

explanation.walkthrough: A theatrical function sounds like a stage party; read instead as the job an actor performs, it is a part in a play.
explanation.definitionFit: Parts played by actors, and more widely the functions people perform.

clue.text: Offers-public sure to be involved

parts.note: overt means open, done in public

indicators.note: being involved means tangled up, so the letters of sure are rearranged

explanation.surface: Proposals are made openly, certain to draw people in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'public' is an adjective (open, overt), not the noun it seems; 'to be involved' scrambles the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtures are opening proposals or approaches made to begin negotiations.

clue.text: In every way made to correspond

parts.note: to tally is to agree or correspond

explanation.surface: Something is adjusted so that it matches in all respects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made to correspond' is 'made to tally'; TO and TALLY join, with 'made' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Completely, wholly, in all respects.

clue.text: Hardy girl, one not so hot as a churchgoer

definitions.text: one not so hot as a churchgoer

explanation.surface: A tough young woman shows little zeal at church.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hardy's novel 'A Laodicean' is named for its heroine, Paula Power; in Revelation the church at Laodicea is rebuked for being lukewarm.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Hardy's novel of that title, and anyone half-hearted in religion, like the lukewarm church of Laodicea.

clue.text: Spots two-gallon vessel on board

indicators.note: on board a ship means inside it, so the vessel goes within the ship's letters

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, the vessel one boards
a peck is a dry measure of two gallons

explanation.surface: Someone notices a two-gallon container being carried aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text reads '011' where the page prints 'on'. 'on' signals the container: being on board a ship is being inside it, and 'board' stands for the ship, SS.
explanation.definitionFit: Specks are tiny spots or marks.

clue.text: Where there's: a ring, maybe gorgeous girls clinch matches?

definitions.text: Where there's: a ring, maybe gorgeous girls clinch matches?

parts.words: Where there's: a ring, maybe gorgeous girls clinch matches?
parts.note: in the boxing ring bouts are won by flooring the opponent; stunning women are called by the same slang word, and might win a wedding ring

explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' is both the boxing ring and an engagement ring; 'matches' are both bouts and marriages.
explanation.definitionFit: Fight-ending blows in boxing, and slang for stunning beauties.

clue.text: Support for retired persons

parts.note: 'retired' looks like pensioners but means gone to bed for the night; the support is the frame holding the mattress

explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' suggests pensioners; here it means people who have gone to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The framework of a bed, which holds up those who have turned in.

clue.text: Tell tales, but not out of school

explanation.surface: A pupil is snitching while still at school.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits as IN FORM: a form is a British school class, so a pupil in form is in school.
explanation.definitionFit: To inform is to report on someone; being in form means being in one's school class.

clue.text: Annoy Rat's friend over the way

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: Mole is Ratty's friend in The Wind in the Willows
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A rat's companion pesters someone across the road.
explanation.walkthrough: Mole and Rat are friends in Kenneth Grahame's children's book The Wind in the Willows.
explanation.definitionFit: To molest is to pester or harass.

clue.text: Set out to determine the course of events

explanation.surface: Someone sets about deciding how things will turn out.
explanation.walkthrough: Echoes the proverb 'Man proposes, God disposes'.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispose is to arrange in order, and also to settle or control how matters go.

clue.text: Place to sleep — somewhat cold for rodents

parts.note: a dorm, short for dormitory, is a sleeping room
ice is a cold thing, frozen water

explanation.surface: A chilly bedroom is offered for small animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Dormice are famous for long sleep, which fits the surface's 'place to sleep'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormice are small hibernating rodents.

clue.text: One trades in the, highest conceptions

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
deals are trades or transactions

explanation.surface: A dealer handles only the loftiest ideas.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideals are standards of perfection, the loftiest notions one can form.

clue.text: A man of spirit-in dire trouble for all that

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other, so the phrase for all that goes within
trouble suggests disorder, so the letters of dire are rearranged

parts.note: still means nevertheless, for all that

explanation.surface: A brave man stays resolute despite terrible difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' scrambles 'dire', and 'in' puts the phrase meaning nevertheless inside the scrambled letters. 'Spirit' is liquor, not courage.
explanation.definitionFit: A distiller makes spirits such as whisky or gin, so he is a man of spirit in the trade sense.

clue.text: Bad quarter quiet. Bad time-altogether

parts.note: a slum is a run-down district or quarter of a town
p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A rough district goes silent during a grim period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altogether' says the joined pieces give the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A slump is a period of sharp economic decline, a bad time.

clue.text: Fists in the House of Lords

explanation.surface: Fisticuffs break out among the peers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dukes' is slang for fists ('put up your dukes'); dukes are also the top rank of peer, sitting in the House of Lords, Britain's upper chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for fists, and the highest rank of the British peerage.

clue.text: Live damned 'comfortably

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for damned, as in d--d
well means comfortably, as in living well

explanation.surface: Someone lives in cursed comfort.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell is to live in a place, reside.

clue.text: A charming accent

parts.note: cute means charming, attractive

explanation.surface: Someone's way of speaking is delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text drops the opening 'A', which the page prints and the wordplay needs.
explanation.definitionFit: An acute is a diacritical mark, as on the e of café.

clue.text: Calculator indicates a slip by, government

parts.note: to slide is to slip
rule is government, the exercise of authority

explanation.surface: An economist warns of a mistake made by the administration.
explanation.definitionFit: A slide rule is a graduated instrument for doing calculations.

clue.text: Girl, having swallowed 4½ gallon cask, is lying down

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so the cask goes into the girl

parts.note: Sue is a girl's name
a pin is a small cask holding four and a half gallons

explanation.surface: A woman who has drunk a whole small barrel is now prone.
explanation.definitionFit: Supine means lying flat on one's back.

clue.text: A tyro': gripped by mad desire to be accomplished

indicators.note: something held in a grip is enclosed, so these pieces go inside the other
mad suggests disorder, so the letters of desire are rearranged

parts.note: L, for learner, stands for a beginner or tyro

explanation.surface: A novice seized by wild longing hopes to achieve something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mad' rearranges DESIRE into REISED, and 'gripped by' puts A and L inside: RE-AL-ISED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be realised is to be achieved or brought to fulfilment.
